Sapere and conoscere in the present

Sapere (to know a fact, to know how) is irregular. Good news: it's conjugated almost like avere, which you already know. Conoscere (to know a person or place, to be familiar with) is a regular -ere verb.

sapereavereconoscere
iosohoconosco
tusaihaiconosci
lui / leisahaconosce
noisappiamoabbiamoconosciamo
voisapeteaveteconoscete
lorosannohannoconoscono

“Seppo” doesn't exist: I know is so. Also remember: sa has no accent (unlike dà), sappiamo has a double p, sanno a double n.

For conoscere, watch the pronunciation, just like leggo / leggi: before o, sc sounds like “sk” (conosco, conoscono); before i and e, it sounds like the “sh” in “ship” (conosci, conosce, conosciamo, conoscete).

", "

Sapere or conoscere?

English has just one verb, “to know”, where Italian has two. The rule of thumb: if you know a fact or know how to do something, it's sapere; if you know a person or a place (you're acquainted or familiar with it), it's conoscere.

sapereconoscere
a piece of information: so che…, so dove…, so a che ora…a person: conosco Marco
a skill + infinitive: so nuotare, sai ballare?a place: conosci Napoli?
Non lo so. (I don't know)something you're familiar with: conosco un buon ristorante
Conosco Giulia, ma non so dove abita.I know Giulia, but I don't know where she lives.
Sai suonare la chitarra?Can you play the guitar? (Do you know how to play the guitar?)

Sapere + infinitive, like volere, potere, dovere

No preposition before the infinitive (no “how to”): so cucinare, voglio sapere, dovete sapere. And don't mix up knowing how (you've learned it) and being able to (you have the opportunity). English uses “can” for both, Italian doesn't:

So guidare, ma oggi non posso.I know how to drive, but I can't today.

Non lo so = I don't know: learn it as a set phrase; the little lo means “it”, literally “I don't know it”. To address a stranger formally, use the 3rd person, as with può: Scusi, sa dov'è la farmacia?

title: Sapere and conoscere
topic: sapere and conoscere; knowing how vs. knowing people and places
why: After volere, potere and dovere, two verbs you'll use all the time to talk about what you can do and who or what you know. English has a single “to know”, so this is a slow lesson on the irregular conjugation of sapere (learners write “seppo” for so) and on choosing between sapere and conoscere, with review of the modal verbs (dovete, voglio).
